title: The 1-Megawatt Rack Debate
gist: Google, Meta, and Microsoft are standardizing 1-megawatt racks through OCP's Mount Diablo project — requiring ±400V DC distribution, Open Rack Wide mechanicals, 3D-IC stacking, and GPU peak currents heading toward 10,000 amps by 2030 — but a credible dissenting camp (Ayar Labs, Quadric, Synopsys) argues thermal density is not a real scaling vector, since optics can spread GPUs across ten 200kW racks for the same performance without re-architecting the data center every two years. Agentic AI is simultaneously converting design assumptions from average power to sustained peak, while one-year market windows against 1.5-2 year spec cycles are pushing billion-dollar accelerator programs to an unsustainable pace.

themes.theme: The rack becomes the unit of design

insights.claim: Google, Meta, and Microsoft are jointly standardizing 1-megawatt rack infrastructure inside OCP through a project called Mount Diablo, built on OCP's Diablo framework and covering liquid management, water flow, and power supply.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Multi-hyperscaler standardization de-risks supplier investment in megawatt-class cooling and power components — watch Mount Diablo spec releases as the demand-timing signal.
insights.quote: Google, Meta, and Microsoft are collaborating within OCP to establish standards supporting the transition through a project called Mount Diablo, based on OCP’s Diablo framework.
insights.locator: At least for now, data center operators

insights.claim: The rack has stopped being a passive enclosure holding independent servers and must now be engineered as a single integrated compute system spanning fabric, liquid cooling, power shelves, busbars, switching, and system management.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: System-level integrators and rack-scale ODMs capture value that previously sat with individual server and component vendors; component-only suppliers get squeezed.
insights.quote: The rack can no longer be viewed as a passive enclosure containing a collection of servers. Instead, it must be designed as an integrated compute system.
insights.locator: Today’s highest-performance AI systems are constrained

insights.claim: Today's highest-performance AI systems are bottlenecked by short-reach, high-lane-count copper connectivity together with the power, networking, and cooling infrastructure required to support it, not by accelerator silicon alone.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Infrastructure — not compute die — is the constraint, so incremental capex flows disproportionately to power, cooling, and interconnect suppliers.
insights.quote: As AI compute density continues to increase, the number of electrical and signaling connections required to scale these systems grows dramatically
insights.locator: Today’s highest-performance AI systems are constrained

insights.claim: Google's 1-megawatt rack architecture centers on ±400V DC distribution inside the data center, explicitly borrowing technology and deployment experience from the electric vehicle industry.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: EV power-electronics suppliers have a direct adjacency into data-center power distribution — an underappreciated cross-sector demand channel.
insights.quote: Central to this approach is the introduction of ±400V DC power distribution within the datacenter, leveraging technologies and deployment experience developed for the electric vehicle industry.
insights.locator: Google was one of the first proponents

insights.claim: Open Rack Wide is roughly twice the width of an ORV3 rack with added structural reinforcement, and AMD's Helios AI rack is built on Meta's ORW specification submitted to OCP in 2025.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: AMD is competing on an open standardized rack platform against Nvidia's proprietary DGX form factor — a strategic wedge for merchant accelerator adoption.
insights.quote: With approximately twice the width of an ORV3 rack and additional structural reinforcement, ORW provides the physical foundation required for next-generation rack-scale AI platforms.
insights.locator: The mechanical infrastructure is evolving in parallel

insights.claim: Nvidia keeps its latest DGX rack-scale systems inside traditional rack dimensions while AMD moves to the much wider ORW form factor, showing the industry has not converged on a single rack-scale implementation.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Data-center operators face incompatible physical footprints between vendors, raising switching costs and favoring whichever form factor wins early site commitments.
insights.quote: Nvidia packages its latest DGX rack-scale systems within more traditional rack dimensions, demonstrating that multiple implementation approaches are emerging across the industry.
insights.locator: AMD adopted this approach with its Helios

insights.claim: Rack power has climbed from roughly four kilowatts twenty years ago to more than 100 kilowatts today, a 25x increase that existing data-center electrical infrastructure was never designed to carry.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: The installed base of legacy data centers is functionally obsolete for AI density — supports the greenfield-build thesis over retrofits for the highest-density workloads.
insights.quote: This trend has grown dramatically from about 20 years ago, when we were at about four kilowatts per rack, where today these racks are pushing more than 100 kilowatts of power
insights.locator: Regardless of the physical form factor

insights.claim: The migration from 12V to 48V and potentially 480V or 800V distribution is driven by a physical constraint, not efficiency preference: existing data-center wiring is not thick enough to carry the equivalent current at 12V and would melt.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Voltage escalation is mandatory, not optional — power-conversion and high-voltage component vendors have a demand floor independent of AI capex sentiment.
insights.quote: But in the existing infrastructure in data centers, the wires are not thick enough to support that much higher level of current. They would melt.
insights.locator: Rather than having 12-volt supplies

insights.claim: GPU peak currents have gone from 100-300 amps in the CPU era to 1,000-2,000 amps today and are expected to reach 10,000 amps per GPU by the end of the decade.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A 5-10x further rise in per-GPU current is a structural tailwind for power-semiconductor vendors like Infineon and for advanced package-level power delivery.
insights.quote: we already see today we are in the range of 1,000 amps, 2,000 amps, and we’re expecting these peak currents to hit 10,000 amps per GPU at the end of this decade
insights.locator: Power delivery is a growing challenge

insights.claim: Because resistive losses scale with the square of current, holding power-delivery resistance constant while doubling peak current quadruples board-level power losses — the mathematical driver behind every architectural change in data-center power.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: I²R scaling is the reusable model for why voltage keeps rising; use it to predict which conversion stages get eliminated next.
insights.quote: Keeping the power delivery resistance the same and doubling the peak current means a factor of four in the power losses, because power losses go with the current squared.
insights.locator: That has big implications for power losses

insights.claim: A 1-megawatt rack fed from a 50-volt busbar would require roughly 20,000 amps through that busbar, which is why 800V-class distribution becomes unavoidable at megawatt density.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Concrete arithmetic showing 48/50V busbars cannot reach 1MW — the mechanical and electrical BOM must change wholesale, creating a replacement cycle.
insights.quote: If you talk about 1 megawatt of power consumption of a server rack with 800 volts, with a 50-volt busbar, you’re more in the range of like 20,000 amps that you need to support through the busbar
insights.locator: Further, the drive toward higher DC power

insights.claim: Efficiency in data-center power architecture is governed by a simple rule — every power conversion step eliminated is a direct efficiency gain — which is the core rationale for whole-facility HVDC.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Vendors whose products are conversion stages face disintermediation; vendors selling the HVDC path capture the consolidated function.
insights.quote: Every conversion step that you can eliminate is again a gain in efficiency.
insights.locator: When moving to high‑voltage DC distribution

insights.claim: By the end of the decade, gigawatt-scale data centers are expected to switch entirely from AC to high-voltage DC distribution across the whole facility, not just inside the rack.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Facility-wide HVDC is a multi-decade infrastructure replacement — a durable demand pool for power electronics far beyond the AI silicon cycle.
insights.quote: we see that there will be a switch from an AC power distribution to a high‑voltage DC power distribution on the complete data center
insights.locator: Further, the drive toward higher DC power

insights.claim: Hyperscaler data-center capacity announcements now arrive daily at hundreds of megawatts to gigawatt scale, making power infrastructure a persistent add-on cost layer to every AI build.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Announcement cadence itself is a demand indicator for grid-side and power-conversion suppliers.
insights.quote: we get the news daily that the hyperscalers plan additional data center capacity in the hundreds of megawatts, or like gigawatt scale
insights.locator: Power delivery is a growing challenge

themes.theme: The contrarian case against megawatt racks

insights.claim: Ayar Labs is explicitly betting as a company against the 1-megawatt rack gaining widespread traction, arguing thermal density is not a realistic scaling vector.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A named commercial bet against the consensus rack roadmap — if correct, megawatt-specific cooling and power suppliers are over-earning on a dead-end architecture.
insights.quote: As a company, we’re betting against the 1-megawatt rack getting widespread traction
insights.locator: Optical adds another piece of the alternative puzzle

insights.claim: Every step up the thermal-density ladder forces a complete re-architecture of the data center's power capacity and even its floor load rating, an unrepeatable exercise that cannot continue to 2, 3, or 5 megawatts.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: The re-architecture cost per density step is the hidden cost that could stall the megawatt roadmap — model it against optics-based alternatives.
insights.quote: It’s not a realistic scaling vector because every single time you do that, you’re re-architecting the entire data center in terms of how much power it can hold, and sometimes even how much weight the floor can hold.
insights.locator: Optical adds another piece of the alternative puzzle

insights.claim: AMD's Helios rack reportedly weighs as much as an elephant, illustrating that structural floor loading — not just power and cooling — is becoming a physical constraint on rack density.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Building structural limits are an underpriced constraint that favors distributed architectures and disadvantages retrofits of older facilities.
insights.quote: You look at AMD’s Helios racks. I believe it weighs as much as an elephant.
insights.locator: Optical adds another piece of the alternative puzzle

insights.claim: Optics can connect 500,000 or more GPUs within a single scale-up domain, releasing physical distance as a design constraint and letting operators spread accelerators across an entire row.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: If scale-up domains reach 500k GPUs optically, the economic case for extreme rack density collapses — a direct threat to the megawatt-rack supply chain.
insights.quote: In that case, length is released as a vector, and you don’t care about it anymore
insights.locator: Optics enables the same number of GPUs

insights.claim: Ten 200-kilowatt racks connected via optics deliver the same performance as a one- or two-megawatt rack without requiring the operator to re-architect power delivery and distribution every two years.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: This is the clean substitution trade: long optical interconnect versus megawatt power/cooling infrastructure. Positioning in one is implicitly a bet against the other.
insights.quote: I achieve the same performance as getting a one- or two-megawatt rack, and now I have to re-architect my entire data center.
insights.locator: Optics enables the same number of GPUs

insights.claim: In data centers, real estate cost is largely irrelevant while power is the true limiting factor — which means spreading GPUs out costs little if the interconnect can span the distance.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Reframes the density debate: optimizing for floor area is optimizing the wrong variable, which undermines the entire rationale for extreme rack density.
insights.quote: You can spread out your GPUs across an entire row, because in data centers, people don’t care about real estate costs so much. Power is the real limiting factor.
insights.locator: Optics enables the same number of GPUs

insights.claim: The semiconductor industry has a decades-long pattern of oscillating between general-purpose compute and application-specific compute, and separately between centralized compute (1960s mainframes, today's hyperscalers) and distributed compute (the 1980s-90s PC era).
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A two-axis oscillation model for predicting the next architecture regime — both cycles are currently at the centralized/general-purpose extreme.
insights.quote: Our industry has a decades-long history of oscillating between chasing general-purpose compute and then pivoting to more application-specific compute that is less general yet far more energy- and cost-efficient
insights.locator: What is the best path forward?

insights.claim: If specialized inference silicon and a pivot back to distributed compute intersect, AI token generation moves into tens of millions of homes and businesses working alongside centralized models, materially reducing the need for endless warehouses of racks.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: The bear case for centralized AI capex: edge inference silicon at scale would cap data-center demand growth. Low probability near-term but high impact.
insights.quote: the need to build endless oceans of warehouses filled with racks can be lessened by deploying AI token generation capability into tens of millions of homes and businesses
insights.locator: What is the best path forward?

insights.claim: Essentially all major CSPs are evaluating 3D-IC design because 1-megawatt racks will require stacked compute dies, whereas 300-kilowatt systems like AMD's Helios are probably not yet 3D-stacked.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Megawatt racks and 3D stacking are coupled — a slip in one delays the other, and both drive demand for hybrid bonding, thermal analysis, and 3D-IC EDA.
insights.quote: Pretty much all of the big CSPs are looking at 3D-IC design because to hit those kinds of densities, you don’t really need 300 kilowatts, like AMD’s Helios
insights.locator: That is where 3D-IC design starts to become

insights.claim: Wafer-scale 'dinner-plate' planar scaling is judged a dead end because of mechanical stress, yield, and the sheer difficulty of moving data across that span — pushing the industry vertical instead of wider.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A direct skeptical read on wafer-scale approaches; capital should follow 3D stacking rather than ever-larger planar substrates.
insights.quote: I don’t think just having a bigger dinner-plate system of wafer-type scaling planar works, because that comes with its own serious mechanical challenges and yield challenges and that sort of thing.
insights.locator: That is where 3D-IC design starts to become

insights.claim: Interposer configurations are expected to move from four dies on an interposer to eight in a four-plus-four stack, or alternatively two-plus-two, with the industry still undecided on which topology wins.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Die-per-package counts drive advanced packaging capacity demand at TSMC-class suppliers; a doubling of dies per interposer roughly doubles packaging intensity.
insights.quote: so we will start to see what was maybe four dies on an interposer either become eight dies on an interposer, with four and four, or maybe just two and two
insights.locator: That is where 3D-IC design starts to become

insights.claim: Two rival accelerator architectures — Google's TPU as one massive systolic-array matrix multiplier with two or four per node, versus GPU-like designs with many smaller cores — will require different stacking approaches, stacking constraints, and different interface and foundation IP.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: IP vendors must fund two divergent roadmaps, fragmenting R&D; conversely it multiplies the number of distinct IP SKUs sold per customer.
insights.quote: Those two strategies will lead to different stacking approaches and different stacking constraints.
insights.locator: That is where 3D-IC design starts to become

themes.theme: Agentic workloads rewrite the power profile

insights.claim: Long-running agentic workflows break the traditional design model of sizing for average power with occasional peaks — for many AI workloads designers must now assume effectively peak power all the time.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Sustained-peak assumptions raise the real power draw per deployed GPU above nameplate averages, meaning grid and cooling demand forecasts built on average utilization are too low.
insights.quote: For many of these AI workloads, you have to assume it’s effectively peak power all the time, so power management and analysis become absolutely critical.
insights.locator: With these long‑running agents

insights.claim: Agentic AI creates irregular and in some cases genuinely 24/7 utilization patterns, forcing systems to be architected for sustained peak operation across the entire power and thermal stack.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: 24/7 duty cycles compress the payback period on efficiency investments and raise the value of thermal headroom in every design.
insights.quote: Agentic AI creates very irregular, and in some cases truly 24/7 utilization patterns
insights.locator: AI/agentic workloads are changing the power profile

insights.claim: The decisive performance metric for agentic AI systems is how fast a processor can save, suspend, and restore a complex model during context swapping, since users switching back and forth cannot be made to wait.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Context-swap speed elevates memory bandwidth and capacity over raw FLOPS in accelerator selection — a bullish read-through for HBM and fast local memory.
insights.quote: The biggest thing about the ultimate metric in terms of agentic AI is how fast a processor or system can save, suspend, and restore a complex model because people might be changing back and forth.
insights.locator: Agentic AI tends to push designs

insights.claim: With everything becoming a die stack, verification must now model physical effects such as thermal maps arising from high switching activity, making the verification side a structurally advantaged part of the EDA business.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: EDA revenue mix shifts toward multiphysics and thermal-aware verification tools — a differentiated growth line inside the EDA vendors.
insights.quote: Everything is going to be a die stack, which means understanding the physical effect of everything you’re doing.
insights.locator: Another added pressure on already extremely complex designs

insights.claim: Packing thousands of GPUs into a rack creates value only if they operate as a coherent computing system, because AI training and inference are increasingly constrained by memory bandwidth, synchronization overhead, collective communication efficiency, and tail latency rather than raw compute.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Density without interconnect improvement yields no application performance — validates spending on UALink-class scale-up fabrics over additional accelerators.
insights.quote: Packing thousands of GPUs into a rack-scale environment only creates value if those GPUs can operate as a coherent computing system.
insights.locator: As rack power scales toward 1 megawatt

themes.theme: Compressed market windows and IP timing risk

insights.claim: AI chip vendors now have roughly a one-year market window per product generation, and missing it means killing that generation outright and moving to the next.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A one-year window makes execution slippage catastrophic rather than costly — schedule risk deserves a much larger discount in accelerator-startup valuations.
insights.quote: They only have a year’s market window to take that product into production. If they miss the market window, they might as well kill that generation and move on to the next one.
insights.locator: Shrinking market windows

insights.claim: Interface IP vendors must have a full subsystem test chip ready by the time a spec is ratified within its 1.5- to 2-year cycle — for HBM that means having a test chip packaged on a co-op substrate with the memory the day a vendor like Samsung releases HBM5.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: IP vendors are effectively funding R&D ahead of ratified standards — a working-capital and risk burden that favors the largest IP houses and squeezes small ones.
insights.quote: The specs are ratified within a 1.5- to 2-year window. We need to have a full subsystem test chip available by the time the spec is ratified.
insights.locator: Shrinking market windows

insights.claim: Accelerator programs now run into a billion dollars apiece, so customers cannot accept unverified or unvalidated IP — raising the barrier to entry for new IP suppliers and concentrating share among proven vendors.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Billion-dollar program costs entrench incumbent IP vendors; risk-averse buyers pay premiums for validated silicon-proven blocks.
insights.quote: These programs are very expensive, running into a billion dollars for an accelerator, so they cannot go wrong on these
insights.locator: Shrinking market windows

insights.claim: A senior Synopsys executive states plainly that running ahead of standards moving faster than the silicon cycle is not sustainable long-term, an unusually direct admission that the current pace will break.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Insider acknowledgment of an unsustainable cadence flags eventual slippage in the AI hardware roadmap — a source of consensus-estimate disappointment.
insights.quote: It’s not sustainable long-term. At some point, this whole madness needs to end.
insights.locator: Shrinking market windows

insights.claim: Advanced packaging materially extends development timelines because the test vehicle must be packaged on a co-op substrate with the memory, consuming months out of an already compressed schedule.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Packaging is now on the critical path for time-to-market, not just cost — packaging capacity constraints translate directly into missed product windows.
insights.quote: And that takes many months, which takes many months off the time you have to get that test chip done.
insights.locator: Shrinking market windows

insights.claim: The workhorse models generating roughly 70% of inference workload are midsize — around a trillion parameters rather than ten trillion — so the majority of tokens are produced by infrastructure with far lower requirements than flagship training clusters.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: If 70% of inference runs on midsize models, the marginal token is served by cheaper hardware than headline capex implies — bearish for the 'everything needs frontier infrastructure' narrative.
insights.quote: But the workhorse models that form 70% of the inference workload are probably midsize — a trillion parameters rather than 10 trillion.
insights.locator: One of the mitigating things for that is models

insights.claim: Frontier training runs and the largest models require a somewhat different infrastructure from workhorse inference, and CSPs already run more than one platform — using Nvidia or AMD for some workloads while operating differently focused internal silicon.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Multi-platform CSP strategies cap any single accelerator vendor's share and support a durable internal-silicon share of the market.
insights.quote: you see with some CSPs, they have more than one platform, and they might use Nvidia or AMD for some things, but they’ve also got their own internal infrastructure that is somewhat differently focused
insights.locator: One of the mitigating things for that is models

insights.claim: Enterprises will not install a 3-ton, 500-kilowatt rack on their own premises, creating a distinct on-prem market segment needing solutions sized to existing IT-room capabilities and workloads that may not even be LLMs.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A structurally separate, lower-density on-prem AI hardware segment exists — addressable by startups and second-tier vendors locked out of hyperscaler sockets.
insights.quote: An enterprise is probably not going to put a 3-ton, 500-kilowatt rack on its own premises.
insights.locator: Wilkinson believes there will be more fragmentation

insights.claim: The compressed development cycle ends through market segmentation and specialization rather than a demand slowdown, with different equipment serving different use cases on less bleeding-edge timelines.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Expect the AI hardware market to broaden into tiers rather than crash — good for diversified suppliers, harder for single-product bleeding-edge players.
insights.quote: The way the madness ends is things settling out into segments and specializations with different equipment for different use cases
insights.locator: Wilkinson believes there will be more fragmentation

insights.claim: The 1-megawatt rack transition is fundamentally an ecosystem integration problem spanning power delivery, cooling, networking, interconnects, memory, optics, software, and facility infrastructure — and the winners will be those optimizing the entire path from grid to chip and chip to chiller rather than any single component.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Favors vertically integrated system players and full-stack EDA/IP suppliers over point-product component vendors in the AI infrastructure value chain.
insights.quote: The winners in the AI era will not be the companies that optimize a single component in isolation.
insights.locator: Cadence’s Khan noted that the transition
